title: A Familiar N+1 Problem: The 26× Speedup from Caching

blocks.1: While operating a sports social platform, I noticed how slowly the feed loaded. Introducing Caffeine caching reduced average response time from roughly 800 ms to 38 ms.
blocks.3:
• Response time: 800 ms → 38 ms, a 95% improvement.
  • DB queries: 81 → 1, a 98% reduction.
  • Throughput: 3.8 req/s → 78.2 req/s, roughly 20×.
blocks.7: There are two kinds of feed items:
blocks.8:
• Completed matches, including results, scores, and reviews.
  • Upcoming matches in matching, scheduled, or in-progress states.
blocks.9: They needed to be sorted as follows:
blocks.10:
• Matches involving friends first.
  • Other matches next.
  • Newest first within each priority.
blocks.11: Each feed item also contains user-specific flags such as isFriend and isMyGame.
blocks.13: A native query using UNION ALL implemented friend-first ordering.
blocks.17:
• 500 matches.
  • 50 users.
  • An average of five friends per user.
blocks.18: Response time
blocks.23: UNION ALL combined four independent query branches. In this query plan, MySQL repeated full table scans instead of eliminating the redundant work.
blocks.26: Lazy loading and additional lookups occurred during DTO conversion.
blocks.32: OFFSET pagination scans and discards rows up to the offset, making later pages slower.
blocks.36: The feed's characteristics were a textbook fit for caching.
blocks.37:
• A read-to-write ratio of 100:1.
  • Completed matches don't change.
  • Upcoming matches change infrequently.
blocks.39: Initially, I wondered whether a ConcurrentHashMap<Long, FeedItemResponse> would be enough.
blocks.41: The issue is memory management. Without explicit removal, entries accumulate. Dozens of new matches each day would require custom eviction logic.
blocks.44:
• maximumSize: Window TinyLFU manages eviction based on access patterns.
  • recordStats: hit-rate monitoring supports tuning.
blocks.45: A tested library was preferable to writing my own LRU implementation.
blocks.49: We had one instance and didn't need network I/O for a shared cache. I chose Caffeine.
blocks.51: [Server startup] ↓ warmupCache() ├─ Completed matches from the last 6 weeks → Completed Cache (max 5000) └─ Upcoming/in-progress matches → Upcoming Cache (max 2000) [Read request] ↓ 1. Load friend IDs (1 query) 2. Read cached feed (0 queries) 3. Sort/filter in memory 4. Paginate ↓ [Response]
blocks.52: The server loads feed data from the DB at startup, then serves that data from memory.
blocks.55: I initially set expireAfterWrite(30, MINUTES), then reconsidered:
blocks.56:
• Warmup only loads data from the last six weeks.
  • Old data isn't loaded in the first place.
  • TTL management added overhead we didn't need.
blocks.57: I controlled memory with maximumSize and left eviction to Caffeine's Window TinyLFU policy.
blocks.60: At first, I cached user-specific fields such as isFriend and isMyGame. That caused a bug: all users shared the cache, so one user's flags could appear for another.
blocks.65: I changed the design to cache only user-independent data and compute user-specific fields at read time.
blocks.72: Warming 500 matches takes about two seconds. Startup gets a little longer, but the cost is acceptable.
blocks.81:
• Before: 81 queries on average.
  • After: one query for friend IDs.
blocks.85: Most work is now in memory.
blocks.88: There is room within the server's 2 GB memory budget.
blocks.96: A restart clears the cache. @PostConstruct warms it automatically, but that takes about two seconds. Redis is a future option if traffic grows.
blocks.98: We currently run one instance. Adding servers gives each its own independent cache, introducing synchronization concerns.
blocks.100:
• Move to Redis.
  • Broadcast invalidation events through Kafka.
  • Consider load-balancer sticky sessions.
blocks.102: Adding or removing a friend must immediately affect the feed. Computing isFriend at read time makes that possible without invalidating the shared cache.
blocks.105: Caching isn't just a speed technique. It's deciding when an expensive computation needs to run once rather than repeatedly.
blocks.107:
• Cache only user-independent data.
  • Compute user-specific data at read time.
  • Warm the cache at startup.
blocks.109:
• Response time: 820 ms → 38 ms, a 95% improvement.
  • DB queries: 81 → 1, a 98% reduction.
  • Throughput: 3.8 req/s → 78.2 req/s, roughly 20×.
blocks.111:
• Longer startup time.
  • Up to hundreds of MB of additional memory.
  • More code complexity.
